title: Disinformation in Facebook Ads in the 2019 Spanish General Election Campaigns
screen_reason: Manual content analysis of the complete corpus of 14,684 Facebook ads posted by the five main Spanish parties during the two 2019 general election campaigns, coded into four mutually exclusive categories, one of which is 'contains disinformation (when ad content is misleading or directly false)'. Reports 292/14,684 ads (1.99%) and 21/1,743 visually identical ads (1.20%) containing disinformation. That is a quantitative share of items judged for veracity (verifiable claims were fact-checked against news media and other sources), so it meets the CONTENT criterion.

estimates.platform: Facebook (paid political ads, retrieved from the Facebook Ad Library)
estimates.date: Pre-campaign and campaign periods for the two Spanish general elections of 2019 (28 April and 10 November)
estimates.measure_type: % of political party Facebook ads whose content contains disinformation
estimates.value_raw: Contains disinformation: 292 total ads, 1.99% of 14,684 (Table 2); 'nor as examples of disinformation per se (292 ads, 1.99% of the total)'
estimates.denominator: 14,684 Facebook ads: every ad in the Facebook Ad Library paid for by the five main Spanish parties (Ciudadanos 8,560; PP 4,517; Podemos 924; PSOE 621; VOX 44; IU 18) during the two 2019 general election campaigns, harvested by a Python crawler
estimates.definition: An ad counted in the numerator if coders assigned it the category 'contains disinformation', i.e. the ad content is misleading or directly false; ads containing verifiable claims were fact-checked against news media and other information sources before being assigned to this or the 'contains facts (not disinformation)' category
estimates.misinfo_def: "disinformation is a phenomenon that deliberately seeks to confuse the receiver with false or misleading information, with the aim of achieving persuasive goals or discrediting an opponent"; the coding category itself is "contains disinformation (when ad content is misleading or directly false)"
estimates.page_loc: Results 4.1 (Use of Disinformation), p. 221; Table 2 ('Contains disinformation: 21 VIAs, 1.20%; 292 total ads, 1.99%')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-author teams coded each variable (one team for the (dis)information variable, one for topic). Inter-rater reliability by Krippendorff's alpha: 0.808 for the (dis)information variable and 0.904 for topic. Verification: 'All the ads that contained verifiable facts were fact-checked through news media and other information sources'; the worked examples in the paper cite press reports and, in one case, the fact-checker Maldita.
estimates.moderator_quote: The object of study were the ads posted on Facebook by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (hereinafter PSOE), the People's Party (hereinafter PP), Ciudadanos, Unidas Podemos [...] and VOX, the five parties with the best election prospects, during the pre- and election campaigns running up to the two general elections held in Spain in 2019.
estimates.notes: Denominator is the full ad census (each microtargeted placement counted separately), so a single disinforming creative that was run against many audience segments inflates this count relative to the unique-creative figure in the next row - the two rows are the same coding on two denominators and only ONE should enter any pooled analysis. sampling_frame=full_census because every ad by these parties in the Ad Library was crawled; denom_selection=curated because the actor set was purposively restricted to the five parties with the best election prospects (an adjudicator could defensibly leave denom_selection empty, since within those actors the corpus is complete). The authors themselves note the Ad Library's transparency may depress the observed rate, since disinformation in ads is easily detected there. Quote replaced with the verbatim Table 2 line ('Contains disinformation 21 1.20% 292 1.99%'); the running-text sentence is split across interleaved print columns ('...nor as examples of disin- / formation per se (292 ads, 1.99% of the total).').

estimates.platform: Facebook (paid political ads, retrieved from the Facebook Ad Library)
estimates.date: Pre-campaign and campaign periods for the two Spanish general elections of 2019 (28 April and 10 November)
estimates.measure_type: % of unique party Facebook ad creatives (visually identical ads) whose content contains disinformation
estimates.value_raw: Contains disinformation: 21 VIAs, 1.20% (of 1,743 visually identical ads) [Table 2]
estimates.denominator: 1,743 'visually identical ads' (VIAs) - the distinct ad creatives underlying the 14,684 ads, each of which was run against different microtargeted audiences with its own spend and impressions
estimates.definition: As the main row: the creative was coded 'contains disinformation', i.e. its content is misleading or directly false, with verifiable claims fact-checked against news media and other sources
estimates.misinfo_def: "disinformation is a phenomenon that deliberately seeks to confuse the receiver with false or misleading information, with the aim of achieving persuasive goals or discrediting an opponent"; coding category: "contains disinformation (when ad content is misleading or directly false)"
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding teams and procedure as the main row; Krippendorff's alpha 0.808 for the (dis)information variable. The manual content analysis was in fact performed on the VIAs ('To perform the analysis, only these VIAs (1,743) were used'), with the total-ad figures obtained by propagating each creative's code to all its placements.
estimates.moderator_quote: Following an initial data analysis, it was noted that there were numerous repetitions in the ad content. This was due to the microtargeting capabilities of Facebook: The same content was used in multiple ads, each with a different sociodemographic audience profile, which will be referred to hereinafter as 'visually identical ads' (VIAs). [...] To perform the analysis, only these VIAs (1,743) were used.
estimates.notes: De-duplicated denominator for the SAME coding as the previous row: 21 unique disinforming creatives out of 1,743, versus 292 of 14,684 placements. This is the unit the coders actually judged, so it is arguably the cleaner content-prevalence figure; the 1.99% row is the paper's headline. definition_variant is false because the veracity definition is identical - only the denominator differs. Do not pool both rows together. Quote is the verbatim Table 2 line, without the added table-caption gloss that made the previous string non-verbatim.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'Reports disinformation' (a party presenting itself as a victim of disinformation): 11/1,743 VIAs (0.63%) and 12/14,684 ads (0.08%). Not extracted: this codes meta-discourse about disinformation, not content that is itself false, so it is not a prevalence estimate for this review. (2) Party-level breakdowns (Tables 3, 4 and 6) were NOT entered as rows even though party subgroups can be a headline, because their denominators are inconsistent and partly unstated. In Table 3 the 'Total' column is corpus-relative (Ciudadanos 1.89, PP 0.06, Podemos 0.02, VOX 0.02, summing to the overall 1.99%), whereas in Table 6 and the running text the VIA percentages are party-relative ('VOX (13.33% of the total number of VIAs) and Ciudadanos (5.6%)'), and the per-party VIA counts are never reported - Table 1 gives only per-party ad totals (Ciudadanos 8,560; IU 18; PP 4,517; Podemos 924; PSOE 621; VOX 44). Converting a corpus-relative share into a party rate (e.g. 1.89% of 14,684 = 277 ads, 277/8,560 = 3.2% of Ciudadanos ads) would be a computed value with a different denominator, which R8 forbids. An adjudicator wanting party rows would have to derive the VIA denominators, which this text does not supply. (3) Topic breakdowns of disinformation (Table 6: Spain's cohesion 1.55%, democratic quality 0.33%, economic policy 0.05%, feminism 0.02%, others/immigration/pacts 0.01% each, of the whole corpus) are decompositions of the same 1.99% and would double-count if entered. (4) 'Does not contain facts' (83.71% of ads / 78.03% of VIAs) and 'contains facts (not disinformation)' (14.22% / 20.14%) are the complementary categories, not misinformation. (5) Spend and impression totals (about EUR 2.1 million; 285.5 million estimated impressions) are exposure-adjacent but the paper never reports what share of impressions carried disinformation, so no EXPOSURE row could be built - this is the most useful thing the paper could have reported and did not. (6) An unavoidable ambiguity in the VOX description: 'In 15 different ads, most of which were integrated into the same VIA, there were elements of disinformation in two' sits oddly with VOX's 44 ads in Table 1 and with the 13.33% party-relative VIA figure; I did not attempt to reconstruct it.

rob.design: Cross-sectional manual content analysis of a complete advertising census. Frame: a Python web crawler harvested from the Facebook Ad Library every ad, with its metadata (run time, spend band, impressions, demographic and regional targeting), posted by the five main Spanish parties (PSOE, PP, Ciudadanos, Podemos, IU, VOX - Podemos and IU treated separately) during the pre-campaign and campaign periods of the 28 April and 10 November 2019 general elections: 14,684 ads. Because Facebook publishes only banded spend and impression figures, the authors used band midpoints, giving approximately EUR 2.1 million of spend and 285.5 million impressions. Because microtargeting duplicates creatives, the analysis was performed on the 1,743 'visually identical ads' and propagated to all placements. No response rate applies. Coding: two variables (type of information in four mutually exclusive categories; topic in fifteen categories), each coded by a team of two authors; ads containing verifiable claims were fact-checked against news media and other information sources. Inter-rater reliability: Krippendorff's alpha 0.808 for the (dis)information variable, 0.904 for topic; no adjudication procedure is described. Author-acknowledged limits: no ad-segmentation (targeting) analysis was performed, and the Ad Library alone 'is not enough to audit disinformation campaigns', with its transparency possibly depressing the observed rate.
rob.item6_quote: The first is the type of information contained in the ads, which fell into the following two categories: 1) does not contain facts (generic calls to vote or election promises); 2) reports disinformation (the party presents itself as a victim of disinformation, manipulated by the media or its political rivals); 3) contains disinformation (when ad content is misleading or directly false); 4) and contains facts (their interpretation may sometimes be more or less biased, but nonetheless cannot be regarded as disinformation). All the ads that contained verifiable facts were fact-checked through news media and other information sources.
rob.item10_quote: All of which means that only 2% of the ads contained disinformation. This is by no means a negligible proportion, but it does indicate that it is not a technique applied by Spanish political parties across the board, neither as a discursive device to report being victims of disinformation operations (12 ads in total) nor as examples of disinformation per se (292 ads, 1.99% of the total).
